preamble: Literary Kabardian has the labiodental ejective fricative [fʼ] (фӏ) where Adyghe has a labialized sibilant ejective, written шӏу and transcribed [ʃʷʼ] by Wiktionary and Wikipedia's Adyghe phonology article: Adyghe машӏо [maːʃʷʼa] : Kabardian мафӏэ [maːfʼa] 'fire'. Wikipedia's Kabardian language article describes the whole labialized sibilant series of Adyghe, /ʃʷʼ/, /ʒʷ/, /ʃʷ/ and /t͡sʷ/, as having become the labiodentals /fʼ/, /v/, /f/ and /v/ in Kabardian; its non-ejective examples include Adyghe шъуз : Kabardian фыз 'wife' and Adyghe цуакъэ : Kabardian вакъэ 'shoe'. All the reconstructions cited here put a sibilant, not fʼ, in the proto-language, but they differ on what it was. Kuipers reconstructs a glottalized fricative, which Applebaum & Gordon (2013: 9) render as alveolo-palatal ɕʷʼ and Wiktionary writes *ɕʷʼ (*māɕʷʼa 'fire'); Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article writes it ʂʷʼ. Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 197–198) instead reconstruct a labialized glottalized hissing affricate *c̣ʷ, which gives ṣ́ʷ in Bzhedug and Temirgoy Adyghe and f̣ in Kabardian; they eliminate glottalized fricatives from Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian altogether, saying that comparison with the other West Caucasian languages shows them to be secondary (Starling lists Ubykh q̇́ǝ-c̣ʷ- 'to become dirty' beside Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian *c̣ʷa-jǝ́ 'dirty'). On that view Kabardian fʼ need not have passed through [ʃʷʼ], so [ʃʷʼ] here stands for the Adyghe-type reflex rather than a settled proto-form.
